item.title: Stereoselective polysubstituted bicyclo[1.1.0]butane synthesis by rhodium-catalyzed kinetic resolution
item.dc:creator: Xiaolong Zhang
Rongkai Wu
Zhaohong Liu

Paramasivam Sivaguru

item.description:
Authors: Xiaolong Zhang, Rongkai Wu, Zhaohong Liu, Ge Yin, Jiaqi Tang, Paramasivam Sivaguru, Xin Hong, Edward A. Anderson, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 331-339
Abstract: Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) are a distinctive class of strained small-ring carbocycles of growing importance in synthetic and medicinal chemistry. However, the enantioselective synthesis of polysubstituted BCBs remains a largely unsolved challenge. In this study, we report a general chemical platform for the stereoselective assembly of chiral or meso 1,2,3,4-tetrasubstituted BCBs from internal alkynes and carbenes through stepwise [2+1+1’] or one-pot [2+1+1] cycloaddition reactions, respectively. Successful execution of these transformations exploits the combination of triftosylhydrazones (carbene precursors) and chiral dirhodium catalysts. The sterically hindered catalyst Rh 2 ( R -3,5- di PheTPCP) 4 features a confined chiral microenvironment that enables exquisite discrimination between cyclopropene enantiomers, affording highly enantioenriched polysubstituted BCBs through kinetic resolution upon reaction with chiral rhodium carbenes. This chemistry operates under mild reaction conditions, uses readily available starting materials, and exhibits broad substrate scope.

item.title: Regulation of target gene expression by chromatin-associated protein-coding transcripts in plants
item.dc:creator: Lu Han
Yuxiang Yuan
Yujie Liu
Yan Li
Yijun Qi
item.description:
Authors: Lu Han, Yuxiang Yuan, Yujie Liu, Yan Li, Yijun Qi
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Article number: eadz4903
Abstract: Protein-coding transcripts are regarded as intermediates that mediate DNA-to-protein information flow, leaving their noncoding regulatory potential largely underappreciated. Genome-wide profiling of RNA–chromatin interactions in Arabidopsis has uncovered widespread associations between protein-coding transcripts and distinct genomic loci, implying that they possess regulatory functions. Here, we found that BT2 and GSL8 transcripts modulate target gene transcription independently of their protein products through distinct mechanisms. The BT2 transcript represses transcription of its targets CEP2 and MRF4 by forming RNA–DNA triplexes, thereby restricting root growth and promoting flowering, whereas GSL8 acts through a triplex-independent pathway. Our findings unveil intrinsic regulatory activities of protein-coding transcripts, challenging the canonical definition of mRNA function and blurring the functional distinction between coding and noncoding RNAs in the context of genome evolution.

item.title: Modular van der Waals MOSFETs through layer-by-layer chalcogen substitutions
item.dc:creator: Seok Young Min
Hyunje Cho

item.description:
Authors: Seok Young Min, Hyunje Cho, Suk-Ho Lee, Jaeho Choi, Taeho Kim, Jong Yun Choi, Heewon Park, Junsoo Yoon, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 340-346
Abstract: In two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), the local electrostatic field of the chalcogen p -orbitals dictates the crystal field splitting of the transition metal d -orbitals, stabilizing diverse electronic states from semiconducting and semimetallic to exotic topological phases. On-demand substitution of the lattice chalcogens is therefore an efficient route to tuning TMDC electronic phases. Here, we custom-molded van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures by layer-by-layer vapor-phase chalcogen substitution starting from p -type WSe 2 multilayers into which we locally inscribed insulating WO x , n -type WS 2 , and semimetallic WTe 2 . This spatially precise conversion seamlessly integrated distinct electronic phases, both vertically and laterally, into modular vdW semiconductor heterostructures that are otherwise inaccessible. As a demonstration, we integrated WO x /WSe 2 local gate stacks to build ultrascaled metal oxide–semiconductor field effect transistors (MOSFETs), achieving an unprecedented subthreshold swing at subnanometer equivalent oxide thickness.

Authors: Yuan Zhang, Yanhe Liu, Yachuang Hu, Zhenkun Zhang, Jie Du, Lele Cui, Qi Liu, Lin Zhong, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Article number: eadz5323
Abstract: Intelligent behavior involves flexible integration of sensory input and abstract rule knowledge. Dendritic computation has been shown to contribute to top-down modulation of sensory processing; however, whether and how it is involved in flexible cognitive processing remains to be elucidated. Combining a rule-based flexible decision-making task with in vivo two-photon imaging and optogenetics in mice, we found that within single layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the auditory cortex, apical dendrites preferentially encoded the inferred abstract rule and somata preferentially represented sensory stimuli, whereas choice signals were present in both compartments. Optogenetic dendritic inhibition impaired rule-dependent somatic choice coding, supporting a task-relevant integration across the dendritic and somatic compartments. These results indicate that dendritic computation in cortical neurons mediates flexible behavior.

item.title: Gate-tunable chiral spin mode in WSe <sub>2</sub> /WS <sub>2</sub> moiré superlattices
item.dc:creator: Zhexu Shan
Wenjian Su
Kenji Watanabe
Takashi Taniguchi
Shiyao Zhu
Yuanfeng Xu
Yanhao Tang
item.description:
Authors: Zhexu Shan, Wenjian Su, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Shiyao Zhu, Yuanfeng Xu, Yanhao Tang
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 316-320
Abstract: The interplay between many-body and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) effects can lead to previously unobserved phenomena in solids. Chiral spin modes (CSMs) are collective spin excitations that arise from such interplay and connect states with opposite chirality. Here, we report a gate-tunable CSM that occurs between conduction SOC-split minibands in near-0°-twisted WSe 2 /WS 2 bilayers. This mode manifests as a sharp resonance with giant Raman efficiency in the pseudovector-symmetry channel of the Raman spectra. By varying the filling, the CSM transitions from a chiral spin exciton to an excitonic polaron. The spin-flip nature is directly confirmed by the Zeeman effect, and the filling dependence indicates a charge-transfer insulator at unity filling. Our results demonstrate that transition metal–dichalcogenide moiré superlattices are a fertile platform for exploring exotic low-lying collective excitations.

item.title: Engineering ordered two-dimensional defect phases to strengthen structural alloys
item.dc:creator: Andreas Bezold
Manuel Köbrich
Jan Vollhüter
Longsheng Feng
Lukas Amon
Nicolas Karpstein
Yunzhi Wang
Erdmann Spiecker
item.description:
Authors: Andreas Bezold, Manuel Köbrich, Jan Vollhüter, Longsheng Feng, Lukas Amon, Nicolas Karpstein, Yunzhi Wang, Erdmann Spiecker, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 306-310
Abstract: Defects in crystals are usually considered to be consequences of deformation, but they can also be engineered as strengthening features. Planar defects can strengthen structural alloys but usually form only during deformation or service, limiting control over their density, stability, and chemistry. We show that predeformation followed by aging can convert such defects into a designed architecture of ordered defect phases. In a single-crystal cobalt-nickel–based superalloy and a polycrystalline cobalt-chromium-tungsten alloy, this treatment creates dense networks of coherent, atomically thin, ordered defect–confined phases. These increase room-temperature strength by more than 200 megapascals and reduce the superalloy’s minimum creep rate by more than threefold. Electron microscopy and simulations show that local chemical ordering amplifies strengthening and that the ordered defect phases remain shearable while impeding slip transmission.

item.title: Glycan recognition by a plant damage-sensing immune receptor
item.dc:creator: Pedro Jiménez-Sandoval
Owen Kentish
Caroline Broyart
Hyun Kyung Lee
Klara Culjak

item.description:
Authors: Pedro Jiménez-Sandoval, Owen Kentish, Caroline Broyart, Hyun Kyung Lee, Klara Culjak, Uwe Osswald, Meriem Aitouguinane, Emanuele Tettamanti, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Article number: eaec6740
Abstract: Pathogens target and degrade the extracellular matrix surrounding plant cells. A central question is how cell wall–derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) are recognized and integrated to trigger immune responses. We address this question by determining the structure of the extracellular multidomain of the impaired in glycan perception 1 (IGP1) receptor in both apo form and bound to the cellulose-derived DAMP cellotriose. Structural analyses reveal that constitutive interactions of leucine-rich repeat (LRR)–malectin domains preconfigure IGP1 for ligand recognition and that the receptor features a highly specific sugar-binding pocket in the LRR domain capable of distinguishing fine variations in glycan structures. By directly sensing cello-oligomers, IGP1 operates as a cell wall surveillance receptor that links pathogen-induced wall degradation to immune alerting, equipping plants to mount rapid and robust defense responses.

item.title: In situ structure of the human ciliary transition zone links linker defects to primary ciliary dyskinesia
item.dc:creator: Haixia Zhou
Lea Terbeck
Andrew Berical
Marine Brunet
Sven M. Lange
Jacob R. Anderson
Heike Olbrich
Diana Carolin Bracht
item.description:
Authors: Haixia Zhou, Lea Terbeck, Andrew Berical, Marine Brunet, Sven M. Lange, Jacob R. Anderson, Heike Olbrich, Diana Carolin Bracht, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Article number: eaei5957
Abstract: The ciliary transition zone (TZ) regulates ciliary proteome composition, yet its molecular architecture, protein content, and contribution to motile ciliopathies remain poorly defined. We applied in situ cryo–electron tomography and subtomogram averaging to human multiciliated epithelial cells. This approach resolved TZ-specific doublet microtubules at subnanometer resolution and identified nine constituent proteins. We found that epithelial cell transforming 2 like (ECT2L) and double zinc ribbon and ankyrin repeat-containing protein 1 (DZANK1) form the major linker complexes between adjacent TZ doublet microtubules. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in either gene cause primary ciliary dyskinesia. ECT2L and DZANK1 deficiency disrupted TZ architecture, caused microtubular abnormalities and abnormal bulbous ciliary tips, and impaired mucociliary clearance. These findings establish a direct genetic link between TZ defects and human motile ciliopathy and illustrate how in situ structural biology can uncover mechanisms of human disease.

item.title: Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving
item.dc:creator: Caroline Needell
Catherine C. Walker
Jeremy N. Bassis
item.description:
Authors: Caroline Needell, Catherine C. Walker, Jeremy N. Bassis
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 311-315
Abstract: When calving cliffs at the margins of Earth’s ice sheets exceed a critical height, runaway retreat may be initiated in a process called the marine ice cliff instability. However, sufficiently tall ice cliffs have rarely been observed. To address this gap, we measured the characteristics of 15,330 ice cliffs across Earth’s ice sheet margins using laser altimetry. We show that cliff height is highly correlated with mélange thickness, water depth, and crevassing. We found that tall cliffs calve more rapidly than parameterizations assume, but dynamic thinning and retreat into regions with low ice thickness gradients prevent runaway retreat. These observations suggest that model projections may underestimate subannual rates of cliff calving, but that the potential for instability will depend sensitively on additional quantities, not cliff height alone.

item.title: Airflows redefine the cost of aerial transport in the wild
item.dc:creator: Martina Scacco
Jeroen B. Smaers
Yuval Werber
Karen Aghababyan
Eneko Arrondo
Ortwin Aschenborn
Nyambayar Batbayar
Hans-Günther Bauer
item.description:
Authors: Martina Scacco, Jeroen B. Smaers, Yuval Werber, Karen Aghababyan, Eneko Arrondo, Ortwin Aschenborn, Nyambayar Batbayar, Hans-Günther Bauer, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 347-352
Abstract: Fuel economy matters to both animals and machines, as the cost of transport can determine where, when, and how far locomotion is possible. However, established estimates of these values for animal flight come from laboratories and treat the atmosphere as constant, even though free-flying animals routinely extract energy from atmospheric flows. Using high-resolution movement data, we estimate the cost of transport for 50 bird and bat species flying in the wild. Our results revise the classic ranking of locomotion costs, suggesting that flying can be cheaper than swimming though almost as costly as running, depending on interactions between physical environment, morphology, and behavior. Linking transport costs to atmospheric conditions provides a mechanistic basis for predicting how changing windscapes will reshape the energetics, movements, and distributions of flying animals.

item.title: To reverse nature loss, change what drives it
item.dc:creator: David Cooper
Sandra Díaz
item.description:
Authors: David Cooper, Sandra Díaz
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 251-251
Abstract: This week, at the 17th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), delegates from 195 countries and the European Union are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, for a global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an international set of goals and targets adopted in 2022 to tackle the biodiversity crisis. The urgent question before them is clear: What must change now to halt and reverse nature’s decline and put it on a path to recovery by 2030? COP-17 comes as international cooperation is under increasing strain. Extreme weather is intensifying, ecosystem deterioration is creating new security risks, and geopolitical tensions are rising. Yet nature’s decline does not pause for geopolitical instability—it deepens it. That makes effective multilateralism, with North and South as equal partners, more important, not less.

item.title: Structural basis for size-selective perception of chitin in plants
item.dc:creator: Kira Gysel
Simon Boje Hansen
Henriette Rübsam
Husam M. A. B. Alsarraf

item.description:
Authors: Kira Gysel, Simon Boje Hansen, Henriette Rübsam, Husam M. A. B. Alsarraf, Eva Madland, Caroline Baadegaard, Ebbe Engholm, Jeryl Xin Jie Cheng, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 298-305
Abstract: Plants detect microbes through pattern recognition receptors that perceive conserved microbial surface motifs known as microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Lysin motif (LysM) receptors recognize and mediate downstream responses to chitinous MAMPs. In this study, we elucidated the mechanism for the specific recognition of long-chain chitin oligomers and identified a hallmark bridge domain characteristic of the CHITIN PERCEPTION (CHIP) receptor class. Structural analysis of receptor-ligand complexes, biochemistry, and in planta functional studies of inhibitory nanobodies revealed the mechanism of size-selective, high-affinity chitin perception in Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula . Additionally, we identified the CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE (CERK) class as low-affinity, yet essential, co-receptors and propose a mechanistic model for a ligand-induced core signaling heterocomplex. Our findings establish the structural and mechanistic basis of differential chitin perception and receptor complex assembly in chitin-elicited plant immune signaling.

item.dc:creator: Jasper Butcher

Authors: Jasper Butcher, Rohith Krishna, Raktim Mitra, Seth M. Woodbury, Donghyo Kim, Rafael I. Brent, Yanjing Li, Nathaniel Corley, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaeh2982
Abstract: The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. Here, we describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which employs free atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active site architecture incorporating a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases we obtain active catalysts in zero shot 96 construct design campaigns.

item.title: Deterministic generation and distribution of genuine multipartite entanglement in macroscopic acoustic resonators
item.dc:creator: Dian Tan
Guixu Xie

Chilong Liu

item.description:
Authors: Dian Tan, Guixu Xie, Libo Zhang, Yang Xu, Chilong Liu, Haolan Yuan, Zhihua Chen, Chang-Kang Hu, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 321-325
Abstract: Generating complex multimode entanglement is a central goal of quantum information science. However, scalable creation of genuine multipartite entanglement is challenging as it requires excellent control and efficient state verification. We report the generation and transfer of genuine multimode entanglement across two multimode acoustic resonators. We prepare genuine multipartite entangled states involving two, four, and six modes across the resonators with respective fidelities of 0.912 ± 0.003, 0.790 ± 0.003, and 0.570 ± 0.001. We further demonstrate the transfer of two- and four-mode genuine entangled states between the resonators with fidelities of 0.785 ± 0.006 and 0.601 ± 0.006. This hardware-efficient and scalable architecture enables deterministic control and generation of complex multimode mechanical states. Our results push the boundary of quantum control in macroscopic mechanical systems, establishing a pathway toward large-scale mechanical quantum networks.

item.title: Electrically driven chiral emission from plasmonic tunnel junctions
item.dc:creator: Yuanyang Xie
Alexey V. Krasavin
Anatoly V. Zayats
item.description:
Authors: Yuanyang Xie, Alexey V. Krasavin, Anatoly V. Zayats
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6821; Pages: 326-330
Abstract: Chirality plays a crucial role in a broad range of processes, including light-matter interactions in physics, chemistry, and biology, while quantum tunneling provides a promising mechanism for light generation at the nanoscale. By integrating tunnel junctions with chiral plasmonic nanohelicoids, we achieved electrically induced nanoscale generation of chiral light at the single-particle level. The tunneling-driven resonant excitation of chiral dipolar modes of the nanohelicoids results in emission of a vortex light beam possessing both spin angular momentum with handedness selectivity of more than 0.8 and orbital angular momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in sign. Our electrically driven approach offers a means for engineering photon spin generation at the nanoscale, highlighting its potential for next-generation optical components in display applications, as well as quantum information processing and photochemistry.

item.dc:creator: E. Rosenfeld

item.description:
Authors: E. Rosenfeld, C. Gidney, G. Roberts, A. Morvan, N. Lacroix, D. Kafri, J. Marshall, M. Li, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaee7961
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal’s assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing’s most important challenges.

Abstract: Intestinal homeostasis requires tight regulation of stem cell maintenance and differentiation to absorptive and secretory cell types, two major intestinal lineages. Key signaling pathways have been identified, but how they balance cell type composition remains unclear. An endogenous fluorescent Hes1 reporter revealed distinct, cell type–specific oscillation frequencies forming a gradient along the crypt-villus axis, which was modulated by cell cycle phase as well as Wnt (wingless-related integration site)–signaling and Notch-signaling activity. We developed a microfluidic system to modulate Notch-signaling oscillations in organoids and found the oscillation frequency to regulate the balance of cell type composition. This study provides evidence that information for cell fate specification is encoded in the frequency of an oscillatory signal.

Abstract: Chitosan, a major fungal cell wall component, activates plant immunity, yet the underlying perception mechanism remains unknown. In this study, we identified OsFID1, an apoplast-localized DUF26 domain protein, as a chitosan-binding receptor essential for chitosan-triggered immunity. Abstract: Bacterial degradation of marine snow aggregates is a major component of global carbon cycling. Abstract: Fever is a common adverse reaction to vaccination, contributing to vaccine hesitancy and reduced uptake. To understand variation in fever risk, we longitudinally profiled fecal microbiota, oral temperature, and serological markers in 171 healthy adults receiving Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 mRNA vaccines. Fever risk correlated with low-grade intestinal inflammation, increased abundance of flagellated Lachnospiraceae bacteria, and increased flagellin expression prevaccine. Microbiomes from fever-high donors triggered stronger inflammation in human intestinal organoids and drove flagellin-dependent vaccine reactions in gnotobiotic mice. Moreover, microbiome flagellin phenotypes and murine vaccine reactions were modifiable by diet. Consistent with this, human fever risk was associated with self-reported diet and metabolic markers. These findings identify the gut microbiome as a driver of vaccine-induced fever, suggesting that microbiome-targeting strategies could modulate immune tone and improve vaccine side effects.

Abstract: Vast amounts of new data are fundamentally shaping how people manage their lives and do their work. The volume is overwhelming—Google Dataset Search discovers 2 million new datasets every month—and so are the uses by scientists, governments, and the public. Governments across the world are treating data as a strategic asset. But data alone are not enough. Infrastructure must be developed that can provide signals about which data are “fit for purpose” for the increasingly vast number of potential uses. item.title: Insights from more than a year of ongoing episodic lava fountaining at Kīlauea
item.dc:creator: A. F. Flinders
N. I. Deligne
K. Hon

K. J. Lynn

item.description:
Authors: A. F. Flinders, N. I. Deligne, K. Hon, D. T. Downs, K. J. Lynn, P. A. Nadeau, K. Mulliken, J. C. Chang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6820; Article number: aef2931
Abstract: Episodic lava fountaining is rare globally, with only three occurrences from Kīlauea (Hawaii) since 1823. Beginning in December 2024, an eruption within the summit crater, Halemaʻumaʻu, has produced 54 fountaining episodes to date, each lasting typically for hours and separated by days to weeks. Although multiple mechanisms have been proposed, fundamental questions remain about how magma reservoir pressure, conduit permeability, and volatile exsolution control fountaining onset. We present a multiparameter record of episodic fountaining at Kīlauea using modern geochemical, geophysical, and geologic monitoring. These observations revealed systematic correlations between fountaining and summit inflation, enabling unprecedented quantitative forecasts. This eruption will provide new constraints on the timing, evolution, and processes driving episodic fountaining globally, and highlights Kīlauea’s role as a natural laboratory for studying volcanic processes.

item.title: High-fidelity entangling gates and nonlocal circuits with neutral atoms
item.dc:creator: Simon J. Evered
Muqing Xu
Sophie H. Li
Alexandra A. Geim
J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides
Marcin Kalinowski
Dolev Bluvstein
Nishad Maskara
item.description:
Authors: Simon J. Evered, Muqing Xu, Sophie H. Li, Alexandra A. Geim, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, Marcin Kalinowski, Dolev Bluvstein, Nishad Maskara, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6820; Pages: 197-201
Abstract: The generation and manipulation of entanglement with low error are essential in quantum information systems. In practice, two-qubit entangling gates constitute a dominant error source, limiting circuit depths and performance in fault-tolerant architectures. Using a neutral-atom quantum processor, we realized entangling controlled- Z gates with a high-Rabi-frequency smooth-amplitude pulse, employing state-selective readout and qubit reuse for fast calibration, and achieved a fidelity of 99.854(4)%, which improved to 99.941(3)% upon loss postselection, with stable performance for 10 hours. We then used these low-error gates in quantum circuits with coherent atom rearrangement. Performance was benchmarked by creating and disentangling cluster states, and subsequently, we studied nonlocally entangled states with scrambling circuits featuring longer-range connectivity. Our approach provides a route toward deep-circuit, efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation.

item.dc:creator: Mathew Domeier

item.description:
Authors: Mathew Domeier, Leandro C. Gallo, Chloé M. Marcilly, Trond H. Torsvik
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 87-90
Abstract: True polar wander (TPW) is presently occurring at a rate of ~10 centimeters per year, exceeding the mean rate of differential plate motion. Whether this rate is transient and negligible on geological timescales or whether Earth has experienced rapid TPW lasting millions of years is unclear. Paleomagnetic evidence has been used to propose fast episodes of TPW, but limitations of the paleomagnetic record have precluded definitive results. Rapid TPW will induce global sea level fluctuations associated with relative changes in centrifugal potential, offering an independent test. We evaluated this prediction using continental flooding reconstructions and identified multiple robust quadrupolar patterns since 320 million years ago, confirming that protracted rapid TPW has occurred on Earth and that couplings among Earth’s rotational dynamics, mantle processes, and surface environments can be strongly episodic.

item.dc:creator: Christoph Trattner
item.description:
Authors: Christoph Trattner
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 5-5
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving upstream in science. Systems such as AlphaFold have already transformed protein-structure prediction, while newer agentic systems can search literatures, generate hypotheses, write and execute code, interpret results, and automate much of the path from idea to paper. Recent debates have asked how such systems may change scientific progress, surprise, and human understanding. Yet they also change something more fundamental: who—or what—participates in deciding which questions are asked, which evidence is surfaced, and which alternatives survive. As machine intelligence becomes part of science’s epistemic infrastructure, steps must be taken to ensure that researchers who did not build, own, or operate the system can still contest how ideas and evidence became a claim.

Authors: Laura L. Gravelsins, Mateja Perović, Madeline Wood Alexander, Tallinn F. L. Splinter, Andrew J. McGovern, Jennifer S. Rabin, Liisa A. M. Galea
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 60-68
Abstract: Menopause is an important biological transition with up to 72 symptoms that shapes aging trajectories across organs and encompasses ~40% of the female lifespan. Although menopause awareness is increasing, research on strategies for menopause symptom management and optimizing health in the postmenopausal period is lacking. This Review highlights that menopause characteristics, such as type, timing, and symptom burden, influence health outcomes and later-life disease risk. Similarly, menopause hormone therapy comes in >200 varieties that differ by dose, formulation of estrogens and progestogens, and timing, each with their own distinct risk-benefit profiles. These distinctions are often missed in the literature but have considerable repercussions for outcomes. Optimized menopause care necessitates a precision medicine approach that considers menopause symptoms, genetics, and previous hormone exposures.

item.dc:creator: Qiwen Gan
Wei Li
Rachel K. Lex
Zhe Ying
Slobodan Beronja
item.description:
Authors: Qiwen Gan, Wei Li, Rachel K. Lex, Zhe Ying, Slobodan Beronja
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Article number: eaed3065
Abstract: Although tumor protein p53 ( TP53 ) mutations are among the most common lesions in epithelial cancers, how p53 loss drives unrestrained clonal expansion remains unclear. Working with mouse epidermis, we found that p53 suppresses clonal expansion by limiting progenitor self-renewal. Integrating chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, transcriptional analyses, and genetic screens, we identified a p53-dependent network controlling progenitor renewal and differentiation, in which secreted frizzled-related protein 1 ( Sfrp1 ), low-density lipoprotein receptor–related protein 1 ( Lrp1 ), and ubiquitin-specific peptidase 22 ( Usp22 ) were direct targets of p53 and the most genetically upstream components. Their suppression after p53 loss generated a radial gradient of Wnt activity across mutant clones. Genetic manipulation showed that a Wnt activity gradient, rather than uniform elevation, was associated with sustained clonal expansion. These findings identify spatial organization as a determinant of clonal behavior and a mechanism by which TP53 inactivation drives tissue colonization.

item.title: Stationary entanglement of a levitated oscillator with an optical field
item.dc:creator: Q. Deplano
A. Pontin
F. Marino
F. Marin
item.description:
Authors: Q. Deplano, A. Pontin, F. Marino, F. Marin
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 113-117
Abstract: Stationary entanglement between the motion of macroscopic objects and light is a long-standing goal of quantum optomechanics, with implications for both fundamental tests of quantum physics and emerging quantum technologies. We report the generation of quantum entanglement between the center-of-mass motion of a nanosphere levitated in an optical tweezer inside an optical cavity and the electromagnetic field. Using heterodyne detection, we reconstructed the full set of optomechanical correlations and observed a violation of separability bounds between the mechanical motion and a propagating optical mode, demonstrating the distribution of nonclassical correlations beyond the interaction region. The entanglement was generated at room temperature and remained robust over a broad range of parameters. Our results establish levitated optomechanical systems as a platform for continuous-variable quantum communication and for tests of macroscopic quantum physics.

item.dc:creator: Hang Chen
Hao Yan
Chuangqi Zhao
Guangze Yang
Chunyi Peng
Jin Huang
Tianyi Zhao

item.description:
Authors: Hang Chen, Hao Yan, Chuangqi Zhao, Guangze Yang, Chunyi Peng, Jin Huang, Tianyi Zhao, Xuanze Li, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 81-86
Abstract: Enhancing toughness in nanocomposites often involves viscoelastic organic phases, but this typically reduces stiffness. We describe a high-modulus toughening mechanism in mature Cristaria plicata nacre arising from a crystalline organic-inorganic framework composed of aragonite nanorods alternately integrated with intratabular biomolecular crystallites. Due to the critical slip-length effect, these crystalline units approach the theoretical limits of modulus and strength. The nanoconfined biomolecular crystallites function as nanopins at interlamellar interphases, alleviating stress concentrations and enabling cross-scale synchronized deformation, thereby conferring high fracture toughness. Inspired by this mechanism, reconstituted nacre fabricated from regenerated aragonite flakes simultaneously achieved high stiffness and crack resistance. These insights offer a promising pathway toward reliable, high-performance structural materials.

item.title: Ultrahigh piezoelectricity by polaron-defect complexes
item.dc:creator: Liang Shu
Guyang Peng
Xiaoming Shi
Yang Zhang
Sixu Wang
Haijun Wu
Qian Li
Hangren Li
item.description:
Authors: Liang Shu, Guyang Peng, Xiaoming Shi, Yang Zhang, Sixu Wang, Haijun Wu, Qian Li, Hangren Li, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Pages: 118-124
Abstract: Materials capable of delivering giant and rapid piezoelectric responses at kilohertz frequencies are pivotal for advanced electromechanical technologies. However, their development has been constrained by a long-standing magnitude–speed trade-off: Ferroelectrics with intrinsic electric dipoles offer fast response but limited polarization, whereas ionic defect motion generates highly polarizable defect dipoles but responds slowly, limiting kilohertz-rate applications. We overcame this fundamental limitation by devising 8 mole % K-doped AgNbO 3 (Ag 0.92 K 0.08 NbO 3 ) thin films engineered to host dynamically reconfigurable polaron-defect complexes through electro-elastic interactions between small electron polarons and lattice defects. Field-driven multi–unit-cell polaron hopping reconfigures these complexes, producing giant defect polarization, and orders-of-magnitude faster kinetics of polaron hopping (versus ionic migration) enables their rapid response. This synergy leads to an unprecedented field-induced effective piezoelectric coefficient of ~7170 picometers per volt with ~6.2% strain at kilohertz frequencies in engineered silver niobate–based films.

item.title: Mitochondrial carrier SLC25A34 links clock, diet, and temperature control of adipocyte lipid cycling
item.dc:creator: Iuliia Karavaeva
Astrid Linde Basse
Samuel A. J. Trammell
Mohammed Faiz Hussain
Lasse Kruse Markussen
Jesper F. Havelund
Marie Sophie Isidor
Adam Chatoff
item.description:
Authors: Iuliia Karavaeva, Astrid Linde Basse, Samuel A. J. Trammell, Mohammed Faiz Hussain, Lasse Kruse Markussen, Jesper F. Havelund, Marie Sophie Isidor, Adam Chatoff, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6819; Article number: eadz4797
Abstract: Adipocyte lipid metabolism is coordinated by circadian rhythms, diet, and environmental temperature, but how these diverse signals are molecularly integrated remains unknown. We showed that these cues converge on the orphan mitochondrial transporter SLC25A34 to orchestrate lipid cycling. During the sleep phase, the adipocyte clock suppresses Slc25a34 expression through the REV-ERB transcriptional repressors. Entering the active phase, consuming lipid-rich diets, or exposure to cold abolishes REV-ERB repression, and lipolytic signals stimulate Slc25a34 transcription through the peroxisome proliferator–activated receptors. SLC25A34 is proposed to import oxaloacetate into mitochondria, dually supporting the tricarboxylic acid cycle and cytosolic acetyl–coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) production. Elevated cytosolic acetyl-CoA then fuels the synthesis of lipids and promotes the transcription of genes enhancing mitochondrial oxidation. Thus, SLC25A34 confers circadian, dietary, and temperature control of adipocyte lipid metabolism.
